newsitem.title: USA: U.S. corn export sales pick up after slow start.
newsitem.headline: U.S. corn export sales pick up after slow start.

text.p: U.S. corn export sales have begun to pick up steam after a dismal start to the marketing year, analysts said Thursday, but the outlook is not all rosy with tough competition from overseas and waning business from several key customers.

The Agriculture Department reported Thursday that net corn sales in the week ended Nov. 14 hit 1.2 million tonnes, a marketing year high, and that exports reached 1.4 million tonnes, also a best for the marketing year, which began Sept. 1. Sales and exports were fairly strong the previous week.

"It looks like now the pace has turned up," said USDA analyst Pete Riley, citing larger sales and an increase in export inspections. "It was just a very slow start this year and now we're seeing signs of a return to a stronger pace."
Analysts said importers who had been sitting on the sidelines bought as prices began edging up recently, locking in before prices moved higher.
Many foreign buyers built up their positions last summer when the size of the U.S. crop was uncertain and only now need to come into the market, they added.
Sales to Asian customers, especially Japan, Taiwan and South Korea have picked up markedly in the last few weeks, along with some recent increase in sales to Mexico, Egypt and unknown destinations.

"I think some of the foreign buyers who maybe were hoping to see lower prices are saying this looks like a low ... with the harvest basically done, and probably are willing to step up to buy," said Dale Gustafson, senior grains and oilseeds analyst with Smith Barney in Chicago.
Gustafson and others, however, said it is unlikely that U.S. corn exports will hit last year's levels.
"The problem I see is we can't exceed the year-ago level, with each and every week we have continued to lose ground," Gustafson said.
USDA is projecting overall U.S. corn exports at 49.5 million tonnes in 1996/97, well below 1995/96's hefty 55.8 million tonnes, the fourth-largest on record.

The decrease is largely due to smaller exports seen to three countries. USDA cut its estimate for Mexico demand by 2.4 million tonnes after record imports last year, and shaved projected imports to South Korea by 2.0 million tonnes because that country is expected to buy cheaper feedwheat.
China is also seen importing 1.1 million tonnes less of U.S. corn than last year because of a record domestic crop.

Gustafson predicted U.S. corn exports would be further squeezed by an increase in competition and lower demand due to a dramatic increase in foreign-produced coarse grains this year as well as a larger wheat crop.
